issues.legal_issue: A sale accompanied by a separate agreement to reconvey cannot be treated as a mortgage by conditional sale when the condition of reconveyance is absent from the document effecting the sale.
material_facts: The seller executed a registered sale deed transferring the house to the buyer.
Several days later, the buyer executed a separate agreement to reconvey the house if the original price was repaid within the agreed period.
The sale deed and the reconveyance agreement were registered on the same day, but the condition of reconveyance was not included in the sale deed.
The seller sought redemption on the basis that the transaction was a mortgage.
issues.conclusion: The documents read together did not create a mortgage by conditional sale because the condition for reconveyance was not embodied in the sale document.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 58(c) of the Transfer of Property Act, a transaction cannot be deemed a mortgage by conditional sale unless the condition is embodied in the document effecting or purporting to effect the sale. The parties' intention is assessed from the language of the document in light of surrounding circumstances, but the statutory proviso applies when the condition is in a separate document. The Court relied on Chunchun Jha v. Ebadat Ali, Bhaskar Waman Joshi v. Shrinarayan Rambilas Agarwal, P.L. Bapuswami v. N. Pattay Gounder, and Vidhyadhar v. Mankikrao.

predicates.redemption_suit_appeal: A party appeals in a suit seeking redemption of property on the basis that a transfer was a mortgage.
predicates.sale_document_lacks_repurchase_condition: The document transferring the property does not contain the condition that the property may be repurchased or reconveyed.
predicates.separate_repurchase_agreement: The parties make a separate agreement for reconveyance of the transferred property.

issues.definition: When a redemption appeal concerns a transfer whose sale document omits the repurchase condition and whose parties made a separate reconveyance agreement, the transaction is not a mortgage by conditional sale.

issues.legal_issue: A transfer that cannot be treated as a mortgage by conditional sale under the statutory proviso cannot, on the circumstances described, be recast as a usufructuary mortgage merely because possession and rent arrangements accompany it.
material_facts: The sale deed, reconveyance agreement, and rent note were executed close together in time.
The seller continued to occupy the house under a rent note and paid rent to the buyer.
The High Court treated the transaction as a usufructuary mortgage despite finding that the statutory requirement for a mortgage by conditional sale was not met.
The reconveyance agreement formed part of the documents relevant to identifying the transaction's true nature.
issues.conclusion: The transaction could not be held to be a usufructuary mortgage; the High Court erred by excluding the reconveyance agreement from its assessment.
issues.legal_principle: The nature of a transaction must be determined by considering the relevant documents together. A usufructuary mortgage requires delivery of possession to the mortgagee, but an agreement for reconveyance is not normally part of such a mortgage transaction. The Court applied Section 58(c) and the definition of usufructuary mortgage in Section 58(d) of the Transfer of Property Act, and relied on the principles in Chunchun Jha v. Ebadat Ali, Bhaskar Waman Joshi v. Shrinarayan Rambilas Agarwal, and P.L. Bapuswami v. N. Pattay Gounder.

predicates.reconveyance_agreement_exists: The transferee agreed to reconvey the property to the transferor on repayment of the transfer price.

issues.definition: When a redemption appeal concerns contemporaneous transfer and reconveyance documents accompanied by a rent note, the transaction is not a usufructuary mortgage merely on that account.

issues.legal_issue: A court may make a conditional appellate disposition to address a transaction in which the property was transferred for substantially less than its value and the circumstances indicate possible exploitation of financial adversity.
material_facts: The seller had purchased the property for a higher sum several years before transferring it to the buyer for a substantially lower sum.
The buyer separately agreed to reconvey the property for the same low price if repayment occurred within the agreed period.
The parties did not reach a settlement despite an opportunity to negotiate and made substantially different offers.
The Court considered that the transfer price did not represent the property's true value and that the circumstances might reflect an attempt to exploit the seller's adversity.
The Court provided that payment by the buyer would restore the lower courts' dismissal of the redemption suit, while failure to pay would leave the High Court's judgment in force.
issues.conclusion: The Court disposed of the appeal conditionally, requiring payment by the buyer for the lower courts' judgments to be restored and otherwise dismissing the appeal.
issues.legal_principle: The Court invoked the principle that a person's adversity should not be exploited by another and referred to Order 34 Rule 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure and U. Nilan v. Kannayyan. It also relied on the observations in Smt. Indira Kaur v. Shri Sheo Lal Kapoor concerning transactions that may be structured to pressure a debtor into losing property for less than its real value. The Court made a case-specific order to do complete justice without holding that the transaction was a mortgage.
